title: The two rank-one Borels intersect scheme-theoretically in the torus
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine $F$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Let $G$ be reductive and $T\subseteq G$ a maximal torus, as in [def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology]. Let $R(G)$ be the largest smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, where solvable means that successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroup schemes eventually become trivial. Assume every maximal torus of the represented fppf quotient $G/R(G)$ [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] has dimension one [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. There are exactly two Borel subgroups $B^+,B^-\supseteq T$ [def-sfb-borel-subgroup-scheme], and their scheme-theoretic intersection is $T$: for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$, $B^+(A)\cap B^-(A)=T(A)$ inside $G(A)$. This includes nonreduced $A$ and characteristic two.

source.place: Theorem 20.16 (a) implies (b), Proposition 20.18 and Lemma 20.21, printed pp.412--415.

proof.text: Put $R=R(G)$. The algebraically closed field $F$ is perfect (every irreducible polynomial has degree one). Apply [lem-sfb-perfect-solvable-unipotent-torus] to $R$: its smooth connected unipotent subgroup $R_u$ is normal in $G$, hence trivial by reductivity. Thus $R$ is a torus. Conjugation by $G$ on $R$ is trivial by [lem-sfb-connected-action-torus-rigidity], so $R$ is central. Let $q:G\to Q=G/R$ be [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]; it is faithfully flat and finitely presented, with kernel $R$, and $Q$ is smooth and connected. The group $Q$ is semisimple: if $N\subseteq Q$ is smooth connected normal solvable, its inverse image is smooth connected normal by that quotient node. It is solvable because a derived series for $N$ lifts to a series ending in the commutative $R$, and the next commutator kills $R$. By maximality of $R$ the inverse image is $R$, hence $N=1$. By [lem-sfb-smooth-unipotent-solvable], every smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup of $Q$ is solvable and therefore trivial; $Q$ is reductive. Now [lem-sfb-reductive-semisimple-rank-formula] gives $R\subseteq T$ and a maximal torus $S=T/R\subseteq Q$, of dimension one by the assumed dimension of every maximal torus of $G/R(G)$. The subgroup correspondence in [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] identifies $q(T)$ with $S$ and gives $q^{-1}(S)=T$ scheme-theoretically.

source.place: Corollary 17.62(b),(d), pp.372--373; Proposition 17.20, pp.357--358; Theorem 5.55, p.113.

proof.text: The maps $B\mapsto q(B)$ and $D\mapsto q^{-1}(D)$ give inverse bijections between Borels of $G$ containing $T$ and Borels of $Q$ containing $S$. Here are the details. For $B\supseteq T$, its image is Borel by [lem-sfb-quotient-borel-torus-images], and $q^{-1}(q(B))=B$ by the subgroup correspondence because $R\subseteq B$. Conversely let $D\supseteq S$ be Borel. By [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], $P=q^{-1}(D)$ is smooth and connected, since both $R$ and $D$ are. It is solvable: a derived series for $D$ pulls back to a series ending in $R$, and one further commutator kills the commutative group $R$. Choose a maximal smooth connected solvable overgroup $B$ of $P$: a maximal dimension exists, and the strict dimension inequality in [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] makes it maximal under inclusion. Thus $B$ is Borel. Its image is a Borel containing $D$, hence equals $D$. As $R\subseteq P\subseteq B$, the subgroup correspondence gives $B=q^{-1}(D)=P$. These arguments also show that containing $S$ corresponds exactly to containing $T$.

source.place: Proposition 17.20, pp.357--358; Theorem 5.55, p.113; inverse-image argument for a smooth central torus.

proof.text:
Apply [lem-sfb-semisimple-rank-one-tangent-dimension] to $(Q,S)$: choose $\lambda:\mathbf G_m\simeq S$, and write $\mathfrak q=T_eQ$, of dimension three. Regard $\lambda$ as a cocharacter of $Q$. By [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer], its centralizer is $S$. Define $P_\pm=P_{\pm\lambda}$ and $U_\pm=U_{\pm\lambda}$ using [lem-sfb-cocharacter-limit-smooth-structure]. These groups are smooth connected, $U_\pm$ are normal unipotent in $P_\pm$, $P_\pm=U_\pm\rtimes S$, and
$$\mathfrak q=\operatorname{Lie}(U_-)\oplus\operatorname{Lie}(S)\oplus\operatorname{Lie}(U_+).$$
The middle summand has dimension one: in $\mathbf G_m(F[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2)$ the elements based at $1$ are exactly $1+a\epsilon$. Neither outside summand is zero. For example, if $\operatorname{Lie}(U_-)=0$, then $\operatorname{Lie}(P_+)=\mathfrak q$, so [lem-sfb-smooth-subgroup-tangent-generation] gives $P_+=Q$. Reductivity now kills its smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup $U_+$, whence $Q=S$ by the semidirect decomposition, contradicting dimensions three and one. The other sign is identical. Consequently both outside summands have dimension one, and both $P_\pm$ have tangent dimension two.

source.place: Lemma 20.20, first proof paragraph, p.415; Theorem 13.33(a)--(c),(e), pp.265--266; Proposition 17.61(a), p.372.

proof.text: Both $P_\pm$ are solvable. Indeed [lem-sfb-smooth-unipotent-solvable] makes $U_\pm$ solvable, and in $P_\pm=U_\pm\rtimes S$ the quotient $S$ is commutative, so the first commutator is contained in $U_\pm$ and its derived series then terminates. Let $K$ be any smooth connected solvable closed subgroup of $Q$ containing $P_+$. Closed immersions inject tangent spaces, so its tangent dimension is two or three. In the first case [lem-sfb-smooth-subgroup-tangent-generation], applied inside $K$ to $P_+$, gives $K=P_+$. In the second case the same statement inside $Q$ gives $K=Q$, impossible: a nontrivial semisimple group cannot itself be solvable. Thus $P_+$ is Borel, and the same proof applies to $P_-$. They are distinct because their tangent spaces contain respectively the nonzero positive and negative summands of step 3. Both contain $S$ by their semidirect decompositions [lem-sfb-cocharacter-limit-smooth-structure].

source.place: Lemma 20.20, first proof paragraph, p.415; Theorem 13.33, pp.265--266.

proof.text: There are at most two Borels of $Q$ containing $S$. By [lem-sfb-torus-normalizer-borel-transitivity], any such Borel is $nP_+n^{-1}$ for some $n\in N_Q(S)(F)$. Conjugation defines a homomorphism from this normalizer group to $\operatorname{Aut}_{F\text{-grp}}(S)$. Its kernel is $C_Q(S)(F)=S(F)$ by [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer]; equality on group schemes follows from the definition of centralizing, not from a test on $F$-points alone. By the character equivalence of [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality] and $S\simeq\mathbf G_m$, its automorphism group is $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf Z)=\{1,-1\}$. Thus $N_Q(S)(F)/S(F)$ has at most two elements. Conjugation by $S(F)\subseteq P_+(F)$ fixes $P_+$, so its normalizer orbit has at most two Borels. Step 4 already supplies two distinct ones, hence they are exactly $P_+$ and $P_-$. The two automorphisms of $\mathbf G_m$ remain distinct in characteristic two, since their characters are the different integers $1$ and $-1$.

source.place: Theorem 20.16 (a) implies (b), p.412; Corollary 17.11, p.355; Theorem 12.9, pp.233--234.

proof.text: Compute the intersection on an arbitrary commutative $F$-algebra $A$. For $x\in P_+(A)\cap P_-(A)$, let $c_x(t)=\lambda(t)x\lambda(t)^{-1}$, a morphism $\mathbf G_{m,A}\to Q_A$. By the defining limit conditions in [lem-sfb-cocharacter-limit-smooth-structure], $c_x(t)$ extends across $t=0$ and $c_x(t^{-1})$ extends across $t^{-1}=0$. For every affine coordinate $f\in F[Q]$, the Laurent polynomial $c_x^*(f)\in A[t,t^{-1}]$ therefore belongs to both $A[t]$ and $A[t^{-1}]$. Uniqueness of the coefficients in a finite Laurent sum gives $A[t]\cap A[t^{-1}]=A$, even with nilpotents in $A$. Hence every coordinate of $c_x$ is constant; evaluation at $t=1$ shows that $c_x$ is the constant morphism $x$. After every $A$-algebra extension and evaluation at any unit, $x$ therefore commutes with $\lambda(\mathbf G_m)$. Thus $x\in C_Q(S)(A)=S(A)$ by [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer]. The reverse inclusion follows from the constant orbit of every element of the commutative torus $S$. This proves $P_+(A)\cap P_-(A)=S(A)$ for every $A$.

source.place: Definitions 13.21, 13.27 and 13.29, pp.261--264; limit-subgroup argument giving Lemma 20.21, p.415.

proof.text:
Let $B^+=q^{-1}(P_+)$ and $B^-=q^{-1}(P_-)$. Step 2 and step 5 show that these are exactly the two Borels of $G$ containing $T$. For every commutative $F$-algebra $A$, inverse images commute with intersections, so
$$B^+(A)\cap B^-(A)=\{g\in G(A):q(g)\in S(A)\}=T(A).$$
The last equality is $q^{-1}(S)=T$ from the subgroup correspondence of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], as applied in step 1. Equality on all test algebras is equality of the closed subgroup schemes. The calculation of step 6 made no reducedness assumption and used integer exponents, so it covers nonreduced algebras and characteristic two.

source.place: Proposition 17.20, pp.357--358; Lemma 20.21, p.415; Theorem 5.55, p.113.

proof_origin.place: Adaptation of Theorem 20.16 (a) implies (b), p.412, and Lemma 20.20, pp.414--415, using Theorem 13.33 to compute the intersection by the two limit conditions instead of the finite-subgroup argument in Proposition 20.18.

lean.statement: theorem rank_one_opposite_borel_intersection {F : Type u} [Field F] [IsAlgClosed F] (G T R Q : Grp (Over (Spec (.of F)))) (i : T ⟶ G) (r : R ⟶ G) (q : G ⟶ Q) (hG : ReductiveTorusCentralizer.IsReductive G) (hT : ReductiveTorusCentralizer.IsMaximalTorus i) (hR : SolvableGroupStructure.IsAlgebraic R) (hQ : SolvableGroupStructure.IsAlgebraic Q) (hr : IsClosedSubgroupScheme r.hom.hom) (hrn : IsNormalSubgroupScheme r.hom.hom) (hRs : Smooth R.X.hom) (hRc : ConnectedSpace R.X.left) (hRsol : IsSolvableGroupScheme R.X) (hRmax : ∀ (N : Grp (Over (Spec (.of F)))) (n : N ⟶ G), IsClosedSubgroupScheme n.hom.hom → IsNormalSubgroupScheme n.hom.hom → Smooth N.X.hom → ConnectedSpace N.X.left → IsSolvableGroupScheme N.X → ∃ f : N ⟶ R, f ≫ r = n) (hq : IsFppfGroupQuotient r q) (hrank : ∀ (S : Grp (Over (Spec (.of F)))) (s : S ⟶ Q), ReductiveTorusCentralizer.IsMaximalTorus s → topologicalKrullDim S.X.left = 1) : ∃ (Bplus Bminus : Grp (Over (Spec (.of F)))) (bplus : Bplus ⟶ G) (bminus : Bminus ⟶ G), IsBorelGroupScheme bplus.hom.hom ∧ IsBorelGroupScheme bminus.hom.hom ∧ (∃ tplus : T ⟶ Bplus, tplus ≫ bplus = i) ∧ (∃ tminus : T ⟶ Bminus, tminus ≫ bminus = i) ∧ (¬ ∃ e : Bplus ≅ Bminus, e.hom ≫ bminus = bplus) ∧ (∀ (B : Grp (Over (Spec (.of F)))) (b : B ⟶ G), IsBorelGroupScheme b.hom.hom → (∃ t : T ⟶ B, t ≫ b = i) → (∃ e : B ≅ Bplus, e.hom ≫ bplus = b) ∨ (∃ e : B ≅ Bminus, e.hom ≫ bminus = b)) ∧ ∀ (A : Type u) [CommRing A] [Algebra F A], Set.range (fun x : StandardGroupSchemes.affine F A ⟶ Bplus.X ↦ x ≫ bplus.hom.hom) ∩ Set.range (fun x : StandardGroupSchemes.affine F A ⟶ Bminus.X ↦ x ≫ bminus.hom.hom) = Set.range (fun x : StandardGroupSchemes.affine F A ⟶ T.X ↦ x ≫ i.hom.hom)
